resident.chief_complaint: Nonproductive cough, chest congestion, subjective fevers, hoarseness, and shortness of breath on ambulation for 2 days.
resident.history: An 82-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of nonproductive cough, chest congestion, subjective fevers, hoarseness, and shortness of breath on ambulation. He had chronic mild neck pain for the past 10 years, treated conservatively. He reported a 6-month history of unstable gait, loss of hand dexterity, and bilateral upper extremity numbness and pain. Laboratory evaluation revealed an elevated white blood cell count, elevated troponins, hyponatremia, and elevated blood glucose. Auxiliary tests showed an abnormal electrocardiogram and elevated right hemidiaphragm with full inspiration on chest radiograph. On hospital day 3, cardiac catheterization revealed extensive stenosis of the major coronary arteries, believed to be the main cause of his dyspnea. On hospital day 5, he underwent triple coronary artery bypass grafting. Despite the cardiac surgery, the patient's dyspnea did not improve. He developed new complaints of generalized weakness and continued to complain of chest discomfort. Magnetic resonance imaging and radiographic imaging of the cervical spine revealed extensive multilevel degenerative spondylosis with moderate to severe central canal narrowing from C2 to C7 and myelomalacia.
resident.physical_exam: On examination, the patient had a grade 3/6 systolic murmur and decreased breath sounds at the bases bilaterally. Spine examination revealed decreased cervical range of motion. Neurologic examination revealed diffuse upper extremity weakness and hyperreflexia in the upper and lower extremities. Hoffman and Babinski signs were negative.
key_positive_signs: Decreased breath sounds at the lung bases bilaterally
Hyperreflexia in the upper and lower extremities
Elevated right hemidiaphragm with full inspiration on chest radiograph
Extensive stenosis of the major coronary arteries on cardiac catheterization
MRI showing extensive multilevel degenerative spondylosis with moderate to severe central canal narrowing from C2 to C7 and myelomalacia
resident.past_history: Medical history included hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease with claudication, benign prostatic hypertrophy, colonic polyps, and multifocal osteoarthritis. He had a 35 pack-year smoking history, discontinued 30 years prior to presentation. He had chronic mild neck pain treated conservatively for the past 10 years.
resident.public_message: An 82-year-old man presented with a two-day history of nonproductive cough, chest congestion, subjective fevers, hoarseness, and exertional dyspnea. He also reported a six-month history of unstable gait, loss of hand dexterity, and bilateral upper extremity numbness and pain, with chronic mild neck pain for ten years. Physical examination showed a grade 3/6 systolic murmur, decreased breath sounds at both lung bases, decreased cervical range of motion, diffuse upper extremity weakness, and hyperreflexia in all extremities; Hoffman and Babinski signs were negative. Laboratory evaluation revealed elevated white blood cell count, elevated troponins, hyponatremia, and elevated blood glucose; electrocardiogram was abnormal and chest radiograph showed elevated right hemidiaphragm with full inspiration. Cardiac catheterization on hospital day 3 demonstrated extensive coronary stenosis, and the patient underwent triple bypass on day 5, but dyspnea persisted and he developed generalized weakness. MRI of the cervical spine showed extensive multilevel degenerative spondylosis with moderate to severe central canal narrowing from C2 to C7 and myelomalacia. Past medical history includes hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease with claudication, benign prostatic hypertrophy, colonic polyps, multifocal osteoarthritis, and a 35 pack-year smoking history discontinued 30 years ago.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description only; the films were not available for review. Cervical MRI/radiographs reportedly showed extensive multilevel degenerative spondylosis with moderate to severe central canal narrowing from C2 through C7 and myelomalacia. The dominant abnormality is multilevel C2-7 canal narrowing. The direction of compression was not stated. These findings correlate highly with the reported gait instability, hand dexterity loss, bilateral upper-extremity symptoms, weakness, and hyperreflexia.

neurology.localization: The myelopathic signs (unstable gait, loss of hand dexterity, bilateral upper extremity numbness and pain, diffuse upper extremity weakness, hyperreflexia in all limbs) localize to the cervical spinal cord, spanning C2-C7, consistent with cervical spondylotic myelopathy. Negative Hoffman and Babinski signs do not exclude this localization.

red_flags.finding: Diffuse upper extremity weakness without long-tract signs (negative Hoffman and Babinski) and no documented sensory level.
red_flags.rationale: Weakness may be compounded by post-surgical deconditioning or critical illness, but the chronic loss of hand dexterity and hyperreflexia point to upper motor neuron involvement. Absence of long-tract signs does not rule out cervical myelopathy, especially in chronic compression.

red_flags.finding: Elevated right hemidiaphragm on chest radiograph.
red_flags.rationale: Could reflect phrenic nerve dysfunction from C3-C5 cord involvement or post-surgical changes, but the dominant myelopathic syndrome is already explained by the C2-C7 stenosis. This finding does not alter the cervical localization or the surgical indication.

red_flags.finding: Persistent dyspnea and chest discomfort after CABG, with new generalized weakness.
red_flags.rationale: These symptoms are likely cardiac or systemic and not explained by the cervical cord lesion. They may affect overall perioperative risk but do not change the indication for addressing the cervical stenosis if the myelopathy is symptomatic and progressive.

red_flags.finding: MRI compression direction not specified (reported as nondiagnostic).
red_flags.rationale: The surgical approach (anterior vs posterior) for multilevel C2-C7 stenosis depends on whether the compression is predominantly anterior (disc/osteophyte) or posterior (ligamentum flavum). Clarifying this is important for planning the decompression.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: No significant mismatch: the myelopathic signs correlate with the C2-C7 stenosis and myelomalacia. Negative Hoffman and Babinski do not contradict the localization.
neurology.public_message: Localization is to the cervical spinal cord (C2-C7) with a high match to imaging. Red flags: (1) diffuse upper extremity weakness and absent Hoffman/Babinski are coexisting and do not exclude myelopathy; (2) elevated right hemidiaphragm is coexisting and likely unrelated to the primary cord syndrome; (3) persistent dyspnea/generalized weakness after CABG is coexisting and does not alter the cervical indication; (4) unspecified compression direction on MRI changes_plan because it may affect surgical approach.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade IV. Intraoperative mean arterial pressure target: 70 mmHg. Blood loss risk: moderate. Prone position tolerance: high risk. Extubation difficulty: unassessable because no airway assessment is documented.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement or further deterioration in myelopathic symptoms (unstable gait, hand dexterity, bilateral upper extremity numbness/pain) after 3 months of supervised conservative treatment (physical therapy, cervical bracing, pain management, and activity modification).
Development of new or progressive neurological deficits, including appearance of Hoffmann or Babinski signs, worsening hyperreflexia, or new bowel/bladder dysfunction.
Radiographic progression on repeat MRI (increased stenosis or worsening myelomalacia) at 3-6 months.
Intractable neuropathic pain or significant functional decline (e.g., loss of independent ambulation, inability to perform activities of daily living).
Evidence of respiratory compromise attributable to cervical cord involvement (e.g., worsening hemidiaphragm elevation or dyspnea due to phrenic nerve dysfunction).
physiatrist_opening.public_message: As the rehabilitation physician, I advocate a structured conservative treatment program for this 82-year-old man before considering cervical decompression, given his high perioperative risk following recent triple CABG and his multiple comorbidities. A 3-6 month trial of intensive physical therapy focusing on gait, balance, hand dexterity, and cervical stabilization, along with pain management and activity modification, is a reasonable first step. However, I must acknowledge that the severe multilevel stenosis with myelomalacia and the 6-month progressive myelopathic symptoms are strong predictors of poor response to conservative care; the literature suggests a conservative success rate of approximately 20% in such cases. Therefore, I propose strict preconditions: if there is no stabilization or improvement in myelopathic symptoms within 3 months, or if new deficits, radiographic progression, or functional decline occur, then surgical decompression should be pursued without further delay. I also recommend clarifying the compression direction to inform surgical planning if needed.

Intractable neuropathic pain or significant functional decline (e.g., loss of independent ambulation, inability to perform activities of daily living).

physiatrist_final.public_message: I appreciate the Deputy Director's recommendation for laminoplasty, but the argument rests on progressive myelopathy and myelomalacia, findings I have already weighed heavily: they led me to propose a low conservative success rate (20%) and strict failure criteria with reassessment at 3 months. However, the patient is 82 years old and only days post triple CABG; a brief cardiac stabilization period is necessary, but a 3-month supervised conservative trial with close monitoring is not 'prolonged' in this context, and it allows time to optimize cardiopulmonary status and assess for any early functional gains. The Deputy did not address the high risk of prone positioning, blood loss, or airway challenges highlighted by the anesthesiologist, nor did they present evidence that waiting 3 months would result in irreversible harm given the absence of acute cord compression and the chronic, slowly progressive nature of symptoms. Therefore, I hold my position: structured conservative care with predefined surgical triggers remains a reasonable first step.

vice_opinions.assessment: 82-year-old man with severe C2-C7 stenosis, myelomalacia, and 6-month progressive myelopathy. Surgical decompression is indicated to prevent further cord injury; conservative management has high failure rate. Recent CABG and ASA IV make perioperative risk substantial, so timing needs cardiac optimization. Without documented sagittal alignment or compression direction, a posterior approach is most conservative if lordosis is present.
proposed_options: Posterior cervical laminoplasty C2-C7 (single-stage, no fusion)
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior cervical laminoplasty C2-C7 (single-stage, no fusion)
disagreement_points: A 3-6 month conservative trial risks irreversible worsening given myelomalacia; I would not support that delay.
Compression direction is undocumented; if primarily anterior, laminoplasty alone may be inadequate. I raise this only as a caution.
deferred_questions_to_director: What interval of cardiac optimization is acceptable before scheduling surgery?
Should standing lateral cervical radiographs be obtained to confirm lordosis before committing to laminoplasty?
vice_opinions.public_message: I recommend posterior cervical laminoplasty C2-C7 as the safest definitive option after brief cardiac stabilization. A prolonged conservative trial is not advisable given progressive myelopathy and myelomalacia.

director_rulings.final_decision: The MRI and symptoms are conclusive. Surgery is indicated. Proceed with posterior cervical laminoplasty C2-C7. Obtain standing lateral cervical radiographs to confirm lordosis, and obtain cardiac/anesthesia clearance within 72 hours; schedule surgery immediately thereafter. Conservative management is rejected.
